_meta.description: Design and growth proposals for the storefront, and the questions that must be answered before each one is decided. Filed 2026-11-19 by session arena/6792f800-zone4. Nothing in this file is implemented by the build; it is the review gate the owner reads before any change is made.
_meta.scope_rule: Proposals are filed here rather than appended to data/suggestions.json so the existing registers and their published counts stay correct; each row cross-references the register IDs it depends on (D-xx, F-xx, AS-xx) and never restates a product value.
_meta.source_rule: Every source link is an official Amazon, FTC, Google or schema.org page. No new product, price, rating, commission, traffic or policy fact is asserted here; where a value is unknown the row says so.
_meta.decision_ids: D-48 to D-60 are reserved for these proposals. They are not written into data/decisions.json by this session: that register is the owner's decision log, and writing 'open' rows into it would change the count published on the Decisions page. A row here becomes a D-row there only when the owner records a choice.

review.note: This page is the review gate the brief asks for: a single place where every proposed change, its cost, its risk and the proof it worked sit beside the twelve questions that must be answered before the change is worth making. Four of them have a dated partial or full application from 2026-11-19 (RD-01 fully; RD-03, RD-06 and RD-08 partly), each labelled with what shipped and what still waits on an answer; nothing else is applied. The thirteen proposals are newly filed here; the site's fifty earlier suggestions stay in their own register (data/suggestions.json) and are not duplicated, so no count on any other page moves. Every source link is an official page; where a fact could not be read from an official source it is marked as missing rather than filled in.

flow.title: Read the twelve proposals
flow.what: Each has its problem, its proposed change, its cost, its risk and the check that proves it worked. Five carry a dated application from 2026-11-19 - one complete, four partial, each naming exactly what shipped and what still waits on you; the rest are proposals only.

flow.title: Answer the twelve questions, or let the defaults stand
flow.what: Each question records what is already known, what is missing, who can supply it and how to discover it. Where a default exists it is named in the discovery step, so silence is still a recorded decision rather than a gap.

flow.title: Mark each proposal Accepted, Rejected or Parked
flow.what: Record the choice with the date in this register (data/redesign.json). Accepted proposals become the next build's scope; the check field becomes its acceptance test.

flow.title: Only then build
flow.what: The build order is the priority order: P1 first, because the tracking-ID test (RQ-02) decides whether any of the rest can earn.

suggestions.title: Give the front page a shopper's headline, not a method statement
suggestions.problem: The hero currently reads “Find the air fryer that fits your counter — with every number fact-checked.” The promise is about the site's checking, not about the reader's dinner. The design register already filed this pattern as anti-slop finding AS-08 (“governance apparatus in the shop window”), and AS-01 records the same habit in article headlines.
suggestions.proposal: Replace the hero H1 and lead with a benefit-first headline and one sentence a shopper would repeat to a friend. Keep a two-line trust row underneath (receipts on every figure / gaps flagged, never hidden) rather than inside the headline. Proposed H1: “Crispy dinners, one counter square.” Proposed lead: “Three air fryers — dual basket, single basket, French-door oven — compared on the numbers their listings state, so you can pick your format in a minute and be sure before you buy.”
suggestions.why: A buyer arriving from search or a link decides in about five seconds whether the page is for them. A headline about the checking method answers a question nobody asked yet; the receipts are the proof, not the pitch.
suggestions.effort: One string pair in scripts/build_site.py plus a rebuild.
suggestions.risk: None to any published product value. The compliance strip and the receipts stay exactly where the gates check them.
suggestions.check: The H1 names a reader outcome; the word “fact-checked” no longer appears in the H1; the disclosure strip still renders above the main content on all pages; scripts/verify.py and qa/audit_site.py stay green.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.shipped_note: The landing-page H1 and lead now lead with the reader's outcome; the receipts moved to the trust row. Article-level headline questions stay with decision D-37.

suggestions.title: Cut navigation from 39 labels to one 9-link primary bar plus a footer directory
suggestions.problem: The single navigation group carries 39 links: the six governance pages, the decision-support pages, the sixteen articles and the RSS feed all sit at the same level. Two of the article labels are full questions, so the sidebar is taller than a phone screen. Nothing here breaks a rule, but nothing reads like a shop either.
suggestions.proposal: Primary bar: Home · Shop all · Air fryers · Meat thermometers · Guides · About · Disclosure. The footer keeps a complete four-column directory that reaches literally every page the site publishes, including the governance and decision-support pages this repository exists to show. The disclosure strip stays under the masthead on every page.
suggestions.why: A shopper needs six destinations; a reviewer needs all of them. A single flat list devalues both audiences. The footer directory keeps the existing “every page reachable” rule intact while the primary bar does the selling.
suggestions.effort: Navigation tables and the footer template in scripts/build_site.py; checks in scripts/verify.py follow the new rule.
suggestions.risk: Medium only if a page loses its only inbound link. The build check must assert every published page appears in the footer directory before the label list shrinks.
suggestions.check: Every docs/*.html appears at least once in every page's footer directory; the primary bar has 9 or fewer links; the single-group rule still holds; no page is orphaned (verify.py asserts it).

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.title: Show the product, not a grey box: a photography gate with a clean fallback
suggestions.problem: No product image appears anywhere on the site. Suggestion S-18 and flag F-43 record why: Amazon images are Program Content and may not be copied or hosted here, and generated or stock photography would misrepresent the product. The result is the one thing a shop cannot be — wordless about what the thing looks like.
suggestions.proposal: Build three independent image slots that each fall back to a labelled placeholder: (1) owner-supplied original photography with a written release on file; (2) listing images rendered live by the Amazon link/API on each visitor's click — never downloaded, never cached; (3) an illustrative, clearly-labelled diagram of the listed dimensions drawn from the dimensions already sourced in this repository. Ship the diagram now, because it is the only route that needs no new permission; switch a slot to photography or live listing images when the owner supplies the release or the API access.
suggestions.why: The visual deficit is the largest remaining “looks generated” signal. A dimension diagram is honest, original, and safe, and it answers the counter-space question better than a glossy photo would.
suggestions.effort: Half a day for the diagram generator; minutes to flip a slot on when a release or API access exists.
suggestions.risk: High if any route is shortcuts. Copying listing images breaches the Operating Agreement's Program Content terms (S-18, F-43). Generated imagery of a real product would also breach the accuracy rules.
suggestions.check: No image file in the repository was downloaded from a listing; every placeholder is labelled; the dimension diagram is drawn only from sourced values and is captioned with its source; the build adds the image to the sitemap for image search.
suggestions.shipped_note: The diagram route shipped: scaled footprint diagrams drawn from the listed dimensions appear on the four category tiles and at the top of each category page (docs/imagery.html records every asset). Photographs still need either an owner release or written word from Amazon (RQ-05).

suggestions.title: Publish one buying page worth ranking: the master buying guide
suggestions.problem: Eight articles each cover a slice. There is no single, long, maintained “best air fryer for most kitchens” page — the page shape that both shoppers and search engines treat as the entrance to a buying topic. The current hub is an index of cards, not a guide.
suggestions.proposal: Publish one master buying guide page, maintained in place: the two-format decision in two paragraphs, then a ranked recommendation within verified facts only (D-12 permits ranking inside sourced facts), then a full comparison table, then the five questions people actually ask, each with a two-sentence answer and a link to the deeper guide. Every claim row keeps its listing source.
suggestions.why: One authoritative page absorbs internal links and search interest that eight thin pages split between them. It is also the page a reader would bookmark, which is the behaviour that turns a click into a purchase.
suggestions.effort: One long page assembled from fact rows that already exist; no new verification needed.
suggestions.risk: Any “best” framing must be traceable to a listed field (D-12, D-19). No test result, popularity or price claim may appear.
suggestions.check: Each ranked statement cites a listed field and a source row; no unit conversion; no price, rating or trend claim; the page appears in the sitemap and the feed.

suggestions.title: One weekly editorial item, published on a named day, with the topic chosen from measured questions
suggestions.problem: The current cadence is one guide every 14 days, and the next topic is chosen by editorial instinct because no search data exists yet. A publication that is never seen updating does not earn a returning reader, and a topic queue built on instinct cannot improve.
suggestions.proposal: Publish one item every Tuesday for eight consecutive weeks: four from the existing queue, four seasonal or question-led pieces written from the same fact rows. Record the topic-selection reason for each one in data/publishing.json. Once Search Console is verified (SG-29), the reason field must cite the query that earned the next topic.
suggestions.why: A predictable day is how readers and crawlers learn that the site is alive. The reason field is what turns the calendar from a wish list into a measured loop.
suggestions.effort: One item per week from existing fact rows; the calendar change is a data edit.
suggestions.risk: Cadence commitments that are missed read worse than no cadence. Each item must still carry its fact table and sources; a thin item should slip a week rather than publish.
suggestions.check: data/publishing.json names the day and the eight dates; each published item has a fact table and appears in sitemap.xml and feed.xml; each has a topic-selection reason.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.title: Annotate every product link with the decision it answers, and add a sticky compare bar on mobile
suggestions.problem: Every product link currently says “View on Amazon” or “Open Amazon link”. A reader who has just read why a format suits them still has to work out which button matches their own case, and on a phone the comparison table is scrolled away by the time they reach the button.
suggestions.proposal: Give each product link a decision label instead of a generic verb: “Best for two dishes at once — see the dual-basket listing”, “Best for a shallow counter — see the single-basket listing”, “Best for hosting — see the 26QT oven”. On mobile, pin a two-button compare bar to the bottom of article pages that returns to the chooser and to the comparison table.
suggestions.why: The label is the last thing a reader reads before leaving the site, so it is the highest-leverage sentence on the page. The sticky bar keeps the decision in reach on the device most readers use.
suggestions.effort: One label field per product and a CSS-only sticky bar; no data change.
suggestions.risk: A label that overstates fit becomes a claim. Each label must repeat a listed field already in the table and must keep rel=“sponsored” and the paid-link label.
suggestions.check: Every shop anchor keeps rel=“sponsored”, the tagged Special Link and the adjacent disclosure; the label text appears in the product comparison table; tap targets are 44px or more on mobile.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: qualify outbound links

suggestions.shipped_note: The decision labels shipped: every product link now names the case it fits (“Best for two dishes at once — see the dual-basket listing”) instead of a generic verb, and each phrase repeats a field already in the sourced table on the same page. The mobile sticky compare bar is still a proposal.

suggestions.title: Publish trustworthy structured data for the store pages
suggestions.problem: Only WebSite and Article JSON-LD exist. The product pages carry no ItemList or Product structured data, so a search result cannot show the store as a compared set of listings — and the site has no way to earn the richer result.
suggestions.proposal: Add ItemList structured data to the shop page and the category pages, listing each product by name, ASIN and listing URL exactly as published. Do not emit aggregateRating or offers, because no verified price or rating exists (F-02). Add Article structured data with author and publisher once the About page exists.
suggestions.why: ItemList is the honest structured-data shape for a comparison page. Emitting offers or ratings the site cannot verify would be exactly the kind of markup Google's spam policies treat as misleading.
suggestions.effort: One JSON-LD builder beside the existing website_jsonld().
suggestions.risk: Structured data is machine-readable claims. Any field that is not sourced must be omitted, not estimated.
suggestions.check: The JSON-LD parses; every URL in it is the published tagged Special Link; no offers, no price, no aggregateRating; Google's Rich Results test accepts the ItemList.

suggestions.title: Name the writer and the method on a real About page
suggestions.problem: Anti-slop findings AS-06 and AS-07 record that no page names a person, an organisation or a method. A byline sentence exists, but there is no About page a reader or a crawler can point to when asking “who is behind this and how is it made”.
suggestions.proposal: Publish /about: who runs the site, that the copy is written with automated assistance and then checked field by field against the listing, what the site will not publish (prices, ratings, trend claims), how corrections are handled, and how to report an error. Link it from the footer, from every article byline and from the disclosure strip.
suggestions.why: Authorship is the cheapest trust signal a small site has, and it is the one Google's people-first guidance names first. It also gives the correction path that an affiliate site is expected to have.
suggestions.effort: One page from data already in data/content.json; a byline link on each article.
suggestions.risk: Low. Claims about how the content is made must match what the repository actually does.
suggestions.check: The About page exists, is linked from every footer and every article byline, names the method accurately, and states the correction path.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.shipped_note: The About page shipped with the production note and the correction path. Naming a person still needs the owner (RQ-06).

suggestions.title: A visible freshness line, only where a date can be verified
suggestions.problem: The footer says “Data observed 2026-11-14” on every page, including pages that were re-read on 2026-11-19. Freshness is the one signal a small site can honestly beat a big one on, and the site currently rounds it down.
suggestions.proposal: Show a per-record “last read” date taken from the verification records that already exist, plus a short “what changed” line on the product pages. Where a date is missing, show nothing and flag it (F-60 does this for the thermometer records).
suggestions.why: A dated observation is the site's whole editorial premise. Showing the newest verified date is free credibility; showing a stale blanket date is a missed one.
suggestions.effort: One rendering change driven by existing dates in data/products.json and data/verification-session-*.json.
suggestions.risk: Do not invent a date for anything unread. A page with no recorded read date must say so.
suggestions.check: Every date under the freshness line resolves to a dated record in data/; no page shows a date newer than its own verification record.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.title: One seasonal hub per season, dated and archived
suggestions.problem: The holiday guide exists as a single article. Seasonal traffic arrives on a predictable schedule, and a hub that is rebuilt each season accumulates links and rank instead of starting from zero every year.
suggestions.proposal: Create a seasonal hub page (“Gifts”) that is rewritten each season and kept at one stable URL, with the season and the date stated on the page. Archive the prior season's version under its own dated URL.
suggestions.why: A stable seasonal URL is how a small site compounds a recurring search peak. Dating the season keeps it honest.
suggestions.effort: One template, one hub page per season.
suggestions.risk: Seasonal framing may not become a popularity claim; D-19's dated-snapshot rule applies.
suggestions.check: The hub states its season and date; prior seasons stay reachable; no trend or sales-rank claim appears.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.title: Rewrite the summary paragraphs so they answer instead of restating
suggestions.problem: Anti-slop finding AS-09 records paragraphs that re-list values the table directly above already states. The reader is told the same number twice and learns nothing the second time.
suggestions.proposal: Where a table already carries a value, replace the paragraph with the judgement the table cannot make: which value matters for which cook, and what it would cost to get it wrong. Delete any sentence whose only content is a number already on the page.
suggestions.why: It is the difference between a listing with commentary and an article. It also shortens every page, which helps the mobile reader.
suggestions.effort: An editorial pass over the eight published articles and the guides; no data change.
suggestions.risk: Judgements must still resolve to a sourced field (D-12); the pass must not introduce a claim without a row.
suggestions.check: No paragraph restates a value already present in the same page's table without adding a judgement; every judgement resolves to a fact row; verify.py stays green.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

suggestions.title: Ship one image per page, sized and captioned, with alt text that describes the decision
suggestions.problem: No page carries an image, so no page can appear in image results and every social share is a bare link. The visual deficit is also the strongest “generated” signal left after the copy pass.
suggestions.proposal: Ship the dimension diagram from RD-03 first, one per category page, drawn from sourced dimensions with a caption and alt text that describes the trade-off (“26QT oven footprint 16.9in deep against 12.75in for the 8-quart basket”). Add an Open Graph image generated from the same template so shared links show the comparison.
suggestions.why: Images are the only part of a page a reader sees before reading. A diagram that compares footprints does more selling than a stock photo of a kitchen ever could.
suggestions.effort: One SVG template fed by data; one OG image route.
suggestions.risk: Same gate as RD-03: original or licensed only, never copied listing imagery, never generated imagery of a real product.
suggestions.check: Every image has alt text and a caption naming its source values; no image is byte-identical to a listing asset; the sitemap lists the images for image search.

suggestions.title: Make the decision surfaces a reading experience, not a table dump
suggestions.problem: The Suggestions page is 14,210 words, the Decisions page 11,410 and the Flagged page 15,842. Each is a single flat document. A reviewer opening it on a phone has no way to work through it, and a first-time reader has no summary.
suggestions.proposal: Give each of those pages a one-screen summary (counts, the five that matter now, the cost of each), then keep the full register behind anchored sections with sticky filters. Add a printable one-page review sheet for the owner.
suggestions.why: The review gate only works if a person can actually finish it. The current pages are complete and unusable at the same time.
suggestions.effort: One summary block per page plus CSS; no data change.
suggestions.risk: None to published values; the counts must be computed from the registers, never typed.
suggestions.check: The summary counts equal the register lengths; every register row is still reachable by anchor; the page still validates.

sources.ref: Google Search Central: helpful, people-first content

questions.question: Is this a shop that shows its homework, or a research register that happens to sell?
questions.why_it_matters: Every other choice — navigation, hero, how much governance is visible, how many selling surfaces exist — follows from this one answer. Today the site is built as both, which is why neither reads cleanly.
questions.known: The brief asks for a polished marketing affiliate site that still publishes its verification. The repository's D-18/D-20/D-21 recorded the warm editorial direction and D-12 allowed the copy to conclude and rank within verified facts.
questions.missing: A single stated priority for when the two goals conflict.
questions.discover: One sentence in the brief. Default if unanswered: shop first, register one click away (the build in this branch's proposals).

questions.question: Is the tracking ID shopnow047c-20 registered and active on an enrolled Associates account for this site's marketplace?
questions.why_it_matters: If it is not, every click on every product link is unattributable and no commission can ever be earned, however good the design. This is the only question whose answer decides whether the site can make money at all.
questions.known: The ID was supplied by the owner and is published on every link as the tag parameter. Format matches Participation Requirements 2(b). Its registration is unconfirmed (F-57, Q-50).
questions.missing: An Associates Central read of the tracking-ID list, and one attributed click in the reports.
questions.discover: The five-step one-link test in data/associates.json, S-39: confirm the ID in Account Settings, build one Special Link per product, click it once, check Today's Earnings after 24-48 hours, record the result.
questions.blocks: Any revenue claim; RD-06's labels are harmless without it, but the site earns nothing

questions.question: Do we have, or can we get, Creators API access for prices and ratings?
questions.why_it_matters: Price is the single field a shopper looks for first. The site withholds it by rule (F-02), and that rule is correct only while no lawful source exists. API access is that source.
questions.known: Participation Requirements allow prices and ratings when they come from an approved API or when Amazon serves them through the link. No access is connected.
questions.missing: Whether the owner's Associates account is approved for the Creators API, and on which marketplaces.
questions.who: Site owner (applies in Associates Central); Amazon approves.
questions.discover: Apply for the Creators API; record the approval date and the permitted fields. If declined, the withholding rule stands and should be stated on the page.
questions.blocks: RD-07 (offers markup), any price display, any rating display

sources.ref: Program Policies: permitted use of content

questions.question: Are the five submitted short links the links the owner intends to promote, or stand-ins?
questions.why_it_matters: The site now publishes five products, two of which are meat thermometers — outside the air-fryer scope of the original brief. Whether that is intended decides the whole site architecture.
questions.known: All five resolve to specific ASINs, re-read on 2026-11-19, with a product-intent record kept separately from the observed redirect. Their compliance status is unresolved, not judged (Zone3 FLG-003).
questions.missing: The owner's confirmation that the five destinations are the intended products, and whether the thermometer pair should stay.
questions.discover: One confirmation message; the site already records both fields separately so nothing needs re-reading.
questions.blocks: Category architecture, the master buying guide's scope (RD-04), seasonal hubs

questions.question: Will the owner supply original photography, or written permission to show listing images?
questions.why_it_matters: Images are the largest remaining gap between this site and a polished shop (RD-03, RD-12). Neither route can be taken without the owner, and one of them cannot be taken at all without Amazon's terms.
questions.known: Listing images are Program Content and may not be copied or hosted. Generated imagery of a real product would misrepresent it (S-18, F-43).
questions.missing: Owner-supplied photographs with a release, and/or written confirmation of the API/affiliate image route.
questions.who: Site owner; Amazon for the listing-image route.
questions.discover: Owner ships photos with a signed release, or the API access from RQ-03 shows whether live listing images are permitted. Until then, the labelled dimension diagram is the only honest visual.
questions.blocks: RD-03, RD-12, the Open Graph image

questions.question: Who is the named writer, and what may the About page say about how the copy is produced?
questions.why_it_matters: Anti-slop findings AS-06/AS-07 record that the site names nobody and describes no method. Google's people-first guidance asks for exactly that, and a reader deciding whether to trust a buying recommendation asks it first.
questions.known: The copy is written with automated assistance and checked field by field against official listings. A byline sentence exists; an About page does not.
questions.missing: The name or organisation to publish, and the owner's approval of the method statement's wording.
questions.discover: One paragraph from the owner; the method statement is already drafted in the repository.

questions.question: Will the self-hosted analytics endpoint be hosted, and under what privacy terms?
questions.why_it_matters: Without it, no click, no scroll depth and no guide completion is measured, so the next topic is always chosen on instinct (RD-05).
questions.known: The endpoint code exists (analytics-endpoint/), five events are defined, and the page script stays inert until an endpoint URL is set. Nothing is hosted (F-59).
questions.missing: A host, a retention period, a consent basis, and a published privacy line.
questions.who: Site owner; the hosting decision is theirs alone.
questions.discover: The endpoint is owner-runnable. Set MEASURE_ENDPOINT in scripts/build_extras.py, publish the privacy line, then read the events.
questions.blocks: RD-05's measured topic selection, any traffic or conversion statement

questions.question: Who verifies the site in Google Search Console, and when?
questions.why_it_matters: Sitemap submission and query data are the only first-party evidence of what people search for before they arrive. Every “choose the next topic from measured queries” proposal depends on it.
questions.known: The sitemap, robots.txt and feed are generated and correct. No property is verified and no query data exists (SG-29, D-42 open).
questions.missing: Verification of the Pages host property and one dated export.
questions.who: Site owner (signs in with a Google account).
questions.discover: Verify the property, submit sitemap.xml, read Performance after 14 days.
questions.blocks: RD-05, RD-04's topic choice, any search-traffic claim

questions.question: Is the affiliate disclosure wording, and its placement, approved for every jurisdiction the site serves?
questions.why_it_matters: The disclosure is the site's licence to earn. It is present above the main content and in the footer on every page, which satisfies the Operating Agreement's identification requirement and FTC guidance; what is not recorded is a check against state-level and non-US rules.
questions.known: “As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.” appears under the masthead and in every footer, and every product link carries rel=“sponsored” plus a paid-link label.
questions.missing: A dated review against the jurisdictions the owner intends to serve; California and EU consumer rules differ from the federal baseline.
questions.who: Site owner, with professional advice if the site is to be run commercially at scale.
questions.discover: A checklist review against FTC Disclosures 101 and the applicable state/EU guidance, dated and filed.
questions.blocks: Nothing in the design; gates any claim that the site is “compliant”

questions.question: How often can a new item actually be published, and by whom when the agent is not running?
questions.why_it_matters: RD-05 proposes a weekly rhythm. A cadence nobody can keep is worse than none: the feed shows a stalled publication and returning readers stop.
questions.known: A 14-day cadence is recorded in data/publishing.json, with one queued guide due 2026-12-01. No human publishing role is recorded.
questions.missing: The owner's realistic availability, and whether a scheduled agent run is acceptable.
questions.discover: Choose daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly; the calendar is a data edit either way.

sources.ref: Google: publish for people, not volume

questions.question: May the site recommend one product outright?
questions.why_it_matters: A shopper wants an answer, and search rewards pages that give one. D-12 permits ranking within verified facts, but no published page currently names a single pick, and it is not obvious the owner wants one.
questions.known: D-12 allows conclusions and ranking where every claim resolves to a sourced fact row. The comparison page compares but does not conclude (AS-05).
questions.missing: The owner's yes or no on a single “best for most kitchens” verdict, and the criteria it would use.
questions.who: Site owner; the criteria must be listed fields only.
questions.discover: One decision. The verdict text would cite capacity, footprint and basket format, never a test result.

questions.question: Should the site stay single-retailer, or add a second merchant?
questions.why_it_matters: Staying with one retailer is simpler and keeps the disclosure honest. A second merchant would double the price coverage and the comparison value, but adds a second set of programme rules, disclosures and tracking.
questions.known: S-28 confirms single-retailer for these products. Every link is a tagged Special Link to one storefront.
questions.missing: The owner's intent for the next 12 months.
questions.discover: Decide at the next review; no change needed to keep the current state.
questions.blocks: Nothing now; shapes RD-04 and RD-12
